title: Anti-Terrorism Clarification Act of 2018
official_summary:
Anti-Terrorism Clarification Act of 2018

(Sec. 2) This bill amends the federal criminal code to make three changes to provisions governing civil claims for damages resulting from an act of international terrorism.

First, the bill narrows the limitation on such claims that occur during an act of war. Current law bars claims for international terrorism that occur during an armed conflict between military forces. This bill specifies that designated foreign terrorist organizations and specially designated global terrorists are not military forces.

Second, the bill makes available any asset of a terrorist party seized or frozen under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act for the satisfaction of court-awarded judgments against the terrorist party.

Third, it allows federal courts to exercise personal jurisdiction over a foreign non-state defendant that accepts benefits from the United States (e.g., foreign assistance).

summary.headline: This law clarifies how people can sue for damages from international terrorism, including when terrorist groups can be sued and how their seized assets can pay judgments.
summary.what_it_does: The law changes federal rules about civil lawsuits for damages caused by acts of international terrorism. It says that designated foreign terrorist organizations and specially designated global terrorists do not count as military forces, so the bar on suing over acts during armed conflicts does not protect them. It lets courts use assets of a terrorist party that were seized or frozen under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act to pay court-awarded judgments against that party. It also allows federal courts to hear cases against certain foreign non-state defendants that accept benefits from the United States, such as foreign assistance.

who_it_affects.group: Victims of international terrorism and their families
who_it_affects.how: They may be able to bring civil damage claims in cases where the terrorist group was previously shielded by the armed-conflict limit, and they may be able to collect judgments from seized or frozen assets.

who_it_affects.group: Designated foreign terrorist organizations and specially designated global terrorists
who_it_affects.how: They can no longer rely on the argument that they are military forces to avoid civil damage claims for acts of international terrorism.

who_it_affects.group: Foreign non-state entities that receive U.S. assistance
who_it_affects.how: They may be subject to personal jurisdiction in U.S. federal courts in civil cases because they accept benefits from the United States.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: The law was enacted on October 3, 2018, and the summary does not give a separate effective date.
